answers.children: Norwegian Lundehunds can be good with children when the children are older and respectful. Their small size, alert and curious nature, and independent streak from puffin-hunting days mean they prefer calm interaction over rough play, and their moderate patience suits thoughtful older kids better than toddlers. Living with them requires supervision to prevent accidental injury from their agile contortions. (PawLabs child-friendly score: 6/10)
answers.other-pets: Norwegian Lundehunds can get along with other pets if introduced carefully. Their independent and curious temperament combined with a history of solitary cliff hunting can lead to wariness around other animals, though their small size reduces intimidation. Owners must manage their alert nature to avoid tension, especially with unfamiliar dogs.
answers.exercise: Norwegian Lundehunds need at least one hour of active exercise daily. Bred to scale steep Norwegian cliffs after puffins, they thrive on hikes over uneven terrain, obstacle courses that mimic crevices, and puzzle toys that engage their flexible joints and curious minds. Without enough activity their independent energy turns to destructive chewing indoors.
answers.shedding: Yes — Norwegian Lundehunds shed a moderate amount year-round with seasonal increases. Their medium double coat, shaped by centuries on remote Norwegian islands, releases undercoat that clings to furniture and clothing. The flexibility in their build means they reach odd spots while grooming themselves, yet loose hair still accumulates in a household.
answers.hypoallergenic: The Norwegian Lundehund has a medium double coat that sheds moderately and spreads hair around the house. Its feathering and undercoat release dander with the loose hair, so it is not among the breeds usually suggested to allergy sufferers and no breed is genuinely hypoallergenic. The independent puffin-hunting background leaves this agile cliff dog with no special coat qualities that reduce allergens.
answers.training: Norwegian Lundehunds are not easy to train. Their intelligence is paired with strong independence developed for hunting puffins alone on cliffs, so they often think for themselves rather than follow commands readily. This makes consistent, puzzle-like sessions necessary, though their curious personality can help when tasks mimic their natural agility.
answers.lifespan: Norwegian Lundehunds live 12-15 years. Their small, extraordinarily flexible build from cliff navigation supports activity into later years, yet the extremely limited gene pool from near-extinction in the 20th century brings health robustness challenges that can affect longevity. (PawLabs health robustness score: 3/10)
answers.size: Norwegian Lundehunds reach 13-15 lb and stand 12-15 in tall. Their small, lightweight frame with unique extra toes and 180-degree head-turning joints feels compact yet surprisingly substantial when they contort through tight spaces. This build, honed for navigating narrow crevices on Norwegian cliffs, makes them agile companions in a home.
answers.barking: Norwegian Lundehunds bark moderately. Alert by nature, they use sharp barks to signal something unusual, a trait carried from their role spotting puffins on remote islands. Their curious and independent temperament keeps excessive noise low unless investigating a new sight or sound.
answers.apartment: Norwegian Lundehunds can live in an apartment if their needs are met. Their small size and moderate adaptability suit indoor life, but their alert curiosity and high energy from cliff-hunting ancestry demand daily mental puzzles and exercise to prevent restlessness. Without these they struggle to settle quietly.
answers.first-time: Norwegian Lundehunds are not a good first dog. Their independent streak, serious digestive health issues tied to a tiny gene pool, and specific exercise needs from puffin-hunting history create demands that challenge novices. The rarity and quirky flexible anatomy require experienced handling to avoid frustration.
